editorial.headline: Other Second-Hand Retail: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad retail category is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today. The category covers the retail sale of other second-hand goods not otherwise included within its defined group: a residual but legitimate space for businesses whose trade is in used goods outside the more specifically described retail activities. Its breadth is precisely its character; the activity is defined by what it sells—other pre-owned goods at retail—rather than by a narrower product identity.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is also available across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That makes the national classification accommodating in formal ownership terms, while leaving the commercial proposition to be expressed through the actual used goods being retailed. A founder considering the activity should read that openness accurately: it is a national position, not a guarantee of registration in every location.

Bali is the decisive exception. At the Besar scale, every scope of this activity is assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk in OSS. Under Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium, all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities are blocked for PMA. The result is not a softer local preference or an additional commercial hurdle; it is a block on PMA registration for this activity in Bali. The national allowance for 100% foreign ownership therefore remains real, but it cannot be used to establish this PMA activity on the island.

That distinction matters because the code can look uncomplicated when viewed only through its national foreign-investment status. For a business operating outside Bali, the record supports a fully foreign-owned PMA structure across the listed scales. For Bali, however, the current answer is categorical: the activity is blocked for PMA under the moratorium. The practical reading is to treat the national openness and the Bali restriction as two simultaneously true facts, each governing its own jurisdictional setting.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness remains real, but it cannot be used to establish this PMA activity in Bali.
